description_full: Consolidated Water Co. Ltd., together with its subsidiaries, supplies potable water, treats wastewater and water for reuse, and provides water-related products and services in the Cayman Islands, the Bahamas, the United States, and the British Virgin Islands. It operates through Retail, Bulk, Services, and Manufacturing segments. The company produces potable water from seawater utilizing reverse osmosis technology and supplies water to end-users, including residential, commercial, and government customers, as well as government-owned utilities. It is also involved in design, construction, and sale of water production and treatment plants, as well as management and operation of water production plants, and treatment and reuse infrastructure for third parties; provision of water related consulting services; and production and supply of bulk water. In addition, the company manufactures and services a range of specialized and custom water-related products and systems applicable to commercial, municipal, and industrial water production, supply, and treatment; reverse osmosis desalination, membrane separation, and filtration equipment; and piping systems, vessels, and custom-fabricated components. Consolidated Water Co. Ltd. was incorporated in 1973 and is headquartered in Grand Cayman, the Cayman Islands.

financial_summary: Consolidated Water Co. Ltd. is a small-cap utilities business with a $436M market cap on $132M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 8% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 37%.

The business throws off $33M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 5.5% of the shares.

sect: Its 14% operating margin trails the Utilities median (21%) by 7pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.73x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+5.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.63, it is more defensive than the market.
About $2.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $36.84, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $28.25 to $49.39 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Utilities peers: cheaper on P/FCF 13.1 vs 19.7, richer on P/E 26.7 vs 20.4 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-4%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 7.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $43.00 on average, 58% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 7.9%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.77).
It runs a 37% gross margin and converts 25% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 2.27x, but high accruals (-9.1% of assets).
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $123.7M (28% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 10.5, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 2.0 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.0% over 3 years, 12.7% over 5 years and 8.7% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 27%).
At current returns, reinvesting 65% of profits supports about 8.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 16.3% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 1.1x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 26%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 6.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 37, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 5.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 68%.
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 6 sales over the past year, net $943K sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (2.1% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 28 consecutive years, raising it 9.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 293 employees, each generates about $451K of revenue, 0.4x the Utilities median, and productivity has risen 6.4% a year.
That works out to $113K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $942K (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
